$comment:
Buildings are placed on tiles, cost commodities up front, take build-points of effort to finish, and then act as sites where recipes may be run. workerSlots caps how many workers may be allocated to that building in a single round.

HOW BIG a building's tile is is not written here. It is worked out from the numbers below - the effort it takes to raise, and what it has to hold - through the ground model and ladder in data/buildingtiles.json, so adding a worker slot can grow the tile and the build says so. The one thing a building may say about its own tile is `shortName`: the label printed on the piece, for a name that will not set above the press floor on a 17 mm band. One building needs one today, and the build names any others the day they appear.

categories.name: Extraction
categories.summary: Sits on a terrain feature or deposit and pulls raw commodities out of it.

categories.name: Storage
categories.summary: Adds slots to a town's stockpile.

categories.name: Civic
categories.summary: Trade, order and the machinery of a town.

categories.name: Military
categories.summary: Raising, housing and hiding behind soldiers.

categories.name: Infrastructure
categories.summary: Built onto tiles or tile edges rather than into a town.

buildings.name: Hut
buildings.summary: Four walls and a roof. Houses one worker.
buildings.story: One room, a smoke hole and a door that does not fit. Everybody means to replace it inside the year; half of them are still in it a decade on, roof patched, door still not fitting.
buildings.notes: The cheapest way to add a worker, and the first thing every player builds.

buildings.name: Timber House
buildings.summary: A proper house of sawn lumber. Houses two workers.
buildings.story: Sawn boards, a plank floor and a chimney that draws properly. The difference between this and the hut beside it is one winter, and anybody who has spent that winter can tell you which is which.

buildings.name: Brick House
buildings.summary: Houses three workers, and they are warm: brick-housed workers ignore Cold Snap events.
buildings.story: Brick takes the day's heat in and gives it back at night, which is the whole argument for what it costs. The people inside sleep through the frost that has the hut next door awake and stamping.

buildings.name: Manor
buildings.summary: Houses four workers and one specialist, and scores at game end.
buildings.story: Glass in every window, a name cut over the door and a kitchen garden walled against the wind. Nobody needs one. The point of a manor is that everyone can see you did not need one.

buildings.name: Lumber Camp
buildings.summary: Lets you fell trees on any forest tile within 1 tile, and stores logs on site.
buildings.story: A saw pit, a bunkhouse and a road of churned mud running back to town. It moves every few seasons, always deeper in, and the stumps behind it map every year it has worked.

buildings.name: Quarry
buildings.summary: Cuts stone out of hills and mountains.
buildings.story: A step cut into the hill and taken down a course at a time, so the hole ends up the exact shape of every wall in town. Nobody who has worked one is ever surprised by how much stone a house eats.

buildings.name: Clay Pit
buildings.summary: Digs clay from marshes, river banks and wet ground.
buildings.story: Wet ground opened up and left to weather. The clay comes out grey and comes back red, and the pit fills with water every spring whether anybody wants it to or not.

buildings.name: Sand Pit
buildings.summary: Sand for glass.
buildings.story: A bank scraped back to clean sand and screened by hand. It looks the least of the diggings and it is the one thing the glassworks cannot do without.
buildings.$watersideNote: Desert sand, OR the sand any water leaves on its bank - a sea shore, a lake rim, a river bar. `orWaterside` is an alternative to the terrain list, the way recipes.json site.orWaterside is; `waterside` on its own (the dock, the harbour) is a requirement on top of it. This is the pair of keys the coast terrain used to hide: coast was in the list and meant both things at once.

buildings.name: Mine
buildings.summary: Built directly on top of a revealed mineral deposit. What it produces depends on the deposit under it.
buildings.story: A head-frame, a windlass and a hole going down after whatever the survey promised. The seam decides what comes up. The miners only decide how fast, and for how long.
buildings.notes: One mine per deposit. A deposit is exhausted after its yield total is drawn; flip the deposit token.

buildings.name: Oil Derrick
buildings.summary: Late-game. Pumps crude oil out of an oil field.
buildings.story: A timber tower over a hole nobody can see the bottom of. It makes a noise the whole valley can hear and a smell the whole valley can place, and it pays for both.

buildings.name: Well
buildings.summary: A town without a well or adjacent water cannot draw water at all.
buildings.story: A shaft, a windlass and a stone kerb worn into a saddle by two generations of buckets. The cheapest thing in the book, and the first thing anybody asks about a new site.

buildings.name: Farm
buildings.summary: Four field slots. Each slot holds one sown crop through its growth track.
buildings.story: A long house, a cart shed and fields worked in turn. The steading is the small part of it; what a farm actually is lies outside the fence and changes colour four times a year.

buildings.name: Pasture
buildings.summary: Holds livestock. Animals breed here and can be sheared, milked or butchered.
buildings.story: A run of fence, a water trough and as much grass as the animals can keep down. It costs almost nothing to put up and takes more ground than the manor does.

buildings.name: Orchard
buildings.summary: Takes three rounds to establish, then yields every round without re-sowing.
buildings.story: Three years of doing nothing but weeding, and then fruit every autumn for a lifetime. The people who plant orchards are rarely the people who get the best of them.

buildings.name: Vineyard
buildings.summary: Grapes only, and only on sun-facing ground.
buildings.story: Rows running with the slope, on the side of the hill that gets the afternoon. Vines want poor ground and good light, which is why a vineyard sits where nothing else would pay.

buildings.name: Apiary
buildings.summary: Bees. Honey for mead, and an orchard next door yields +1.
buildings.story: A row of skeps under a hedge and a keeper who has stopped flinching. The honey is the trade; the reason the orchard next door crops heavier is on nobody's ledger.

buildings.name: Dock
buildings.summary: Fishing, and the cheap end of water transport. Goes on any land the water reaches - a sea shore, a lake rim or a river bank all do.
buildings.story: Planks on piles, a bollard, and a boat that leaks slowly enough. It is the cheapest way there is to touch water, and half the towns on the map began as one.

buildings.name: Sawmill
buildings.summary: Logs into lumber. Doubles its rate on a waterside tile - water drives the saw.
buildings.story: A frame saw, a race and a wheel, turning out lengths no one could cut straight by hand in a day. Beside running water it does the work twice over and asks for nothing extra.

buildings.name: Charcoal Kiln
buildings.summary: Logs into charcoal, for smelting where there is no coal.
buildings.story: A covered stack burned slow for a week and watched day and night so it smoulders and never catches. The colliers sleep in shifts beside it and go home the colour of it.

buildings.name: Smelter
buildings.summary: Ore plus fuel into metal.
buildings.story: Ore, fuel and air, and the hill's iron running out of the bottom. The slag heap by the door grows faster than the metal does, which surprises everybody exactly once.

buildings.name: Steelworks
buildings.summary: The refinery. Pig iron plus coal into steel - and it only really works on coal.
buildings.story: Coal, not charcoal - hand it charcoal and it sulks. What comes out holds an edge through a whole season of felling, and every smith within a week's cart ride knows its name.

buildings.name: Brickworks
buildings.summary: Clay plus fuel into brick.
buildings.story: Clay moulded, dried in the open and burned in a kiln that runs for days. A brickworks is mostly stacks: green ones waiting, fired ones cooling, and one being carted away.

buildings.name: Glassworks
buildings.summary: Sand plus heavy fuel into glass. Hot, hungry and profitable.
buildings.story: A furnace that is never allowed to go out, and men working in front of it in leather aprons in high summer. Hot, hungry and profitable, in that order and by some distance.

buildings.name: Blacksmith
buildings.summary: Where every tool in the game is made and repaired.
buildings.story: An anvil, a hearth and a floor of beaten scale. Every tool in the game came out of a door like this one, and comes back through it a little thinner every few seasons.

buildings.name: Carpenter's Shop
buildings.summary: Wooden equipment: ploughs, looms, wheels, barrels, crates.
buildings.story: Shavings to the ankle and every wall hung with patterns. Wheelwright, cooper and joiner are three trades and one bench - and in a small town, one person as well.

buildings.name: Weaver's Shed
buildings.summary: Houses spinning wheels and looms. Fibre in, cloth out.
buildings.story: Looms in a long room with the best light in the building, because the work stops when the light does. The clack of it carries three streets, and the neighbours stop hearing it inside a week.

buildings.name: Tannery
buildings.summary: Hide plus water into leather. Nobody wants it upwind of the town.
buildings.story: Pits, bark stacks and racks of hide drying in the wind. Every town puts it downwind and downstream, and every town would notice inside a month if it were gone.

buildings.name: Tailor
buildings.summary: Cloth and leather into clothing and light armour.
buildings.story: Cloth, shears and a table long enough to lay a bolt out flat. Half the work is the good coat somebody will be buried in. The other half is patching the one they have on.

buildings.name: Mill
buildings.summary: Grain into flour. Free extra output on a hills tile or a waterside one (wind and water).
buildings.story: Stones the width of a cart, dressed by hand every few months, turning on whatever the site will give - a hill's wind or a river's fall. The miller takes a share and is never entirely trusted.

buildings.name: Bakery
buildings.summary: Flour, water and fuel into bread - the most efficient food in the game.
buildings.story: An oven fired once and used all day as it cools, hottest bread first. It turns less grain into more food than anything else in the book, and the whole street knows when it is lit.

buildings.name: Butcher
buildings.summary: Livestock into meat and hide. Salt on hand turns meat into salted meat.
buildings.story: A hook, a block, and nothing wasted. Salt on hand is the difference between meat for this week and meat for the winter, and the butcher will tell you so before you ask.

buildings.name: Dairy
buildings.summary: Milk into cheese, which unlike milk keeps.
buildings.story: Cool, dark and scrubbed back to the grain. Milk is a day from spoiling and cheese is a year from it, and the whole building exists to move one into the other.

buildings.name: Brewery
buildings.summary: Grain or honey, water and a barrel into ale or mead.
buildings.story: Mash, barrel, and a cellar at an even temperature. Ale is grain the town will actually drink; mead is the apiary's honey come back as something worth arguing about.

buildings.name: Winery
buildings.summary: Grapes, water and a barrel into wine. Must be built on or beside a vineyard.
buildings.story: A press, a cellar, and a great deal of waiting. It stands on the vines because grapes will not travel: a day on a cart and what you are making is vinegar.

buildings.name: Warehouse
buildings.summary: Twelve storage slots for anything. A prime target for thieves.
buildings.story: Twelve bays, a strong door and a ledger nailed by the entrance. It will hold anything at all, which is exactly why it is the first place a thief asks after.

buildings.name: Granary
buildings.summary: Ten slots for food and drink only - and food inside it does not perish.
buildings.story: Raised on staddle stones, floor swept, dry and dark and shut against the weather. What goes in comes out the same the following spring, and that is the whole trick of it.
buildings.notes: This is the 'greenery' from the original brief: the building a town feeds itself out of.

buildings.name: Market
buildings.summary: Lets a town buy from and sell to the board at the current price band.
buildings.story: Trestles, an awning and a bell rung at noon. A town puts one up before it can afford anything else, because a stall and an armful of gathered wood is how somebody with nothing starts again.
buildings.notes: Cheap on purpose. The market is the safety net: any player who has lost their tools can gather deadwood by hand, put up a stall, and buy a replacement.

buildings.name: Trading House
buildings.summary: Removes the market spread for its owner in that town, and lets them trade with any player who has a merchant or trading house connected by a route.
buildings.story: A counting room, a strong box, and a clerk who knows the price in four towns without looking it up. What it deals in is not goods but the spread - and to its owner it sells that at nothing.

buildings.name: Town Hall
buildings.summary: Founds a town on a tile and marks its stockpile. One per town, always the first thing placed.
buildings.story: A room, a table and a locked chest, and the first thing anybody sets down. Everything else on the tile is measured from its door, including how much the town thinks of itself.

buildings.name: Guildhall
buildings.summary: Train a worker into a specialist here. One training per round.
buildings.story: A hall, a master, and a set of standards nobody is allowed to write down. A worker goes in able and comes out qualified, which is a different thing and is charged for as one.

buildings.name: Inn
buildings.summary: Rest, rumour and hired muscle. Serve drink to clear unrest; travellers rest here to heal; escorts are hired here; quests are heard here. The one building in the game that may stand outside a town.
buildings.story: A fire, a bench, and beds upstairs that are not quite long enough. Rumour, hired muscle and a night that mends a person - and the one building here that will stand alone on an empty road.

roadside.$comment: An inn is the only building that does not need a town under it. That is not a special case for its own sake - it is what makes a long route survivable, and it is the reason a player builds anything on the empty half of the board. A roadside inn is a holding: it earns, it can be bought and sold, and it can be burned down.
roadside.where: On any tile carrying a road, rail or a route the builder has travelled, in or out of a town. A roadside inn founds no town and stores nothing.
roadside.capNote: Three inns per player. Past that an innkeeper is a landlord, and landlords are the land-ownership rules, which are not written yet.

drink.$comment: The sink the drink half of the economy was missing. Ale is the everyday pour and mead is what an inn actually wants: it is the only thing on the list that both clears unrest and pays a toll back to its owner, which is what makes an apiary and a brewery worth the tiles they sit on.

serves.note: Mead is the inn's own trade. Two unrest a barrel, and no other building will take it in quantity.

drink.limit: One barrel served per inn per round, owner's choice of which.

rest.$comment: Stated on the building as well as in rules.json rest, because the building is where a player looks.
rest.toll: At an inn owned by another player, the 5 coin goes to that player rather than to the board. At your own, it is waived.

buildings.notes: Resting, hireling costs and rumours are in rules.json under rest and hirelings. Every settlement printed on a map is assumed to contain an inn of its rank - those are the board's, not any player's.

buildings.name: Infirmary
buildings.summary: Where the sick are tended and healers are trained. A town with a fed healer weathers illness cards that empty other towns.
buildings.story: Clean linen, a still, and a healer asleep in the next room. In a good year it looks like money thrown away. In a plague year it is why the town is still on the map.

buildings.name: Barracks
buildings.summary: Turns fed workers into soldiers, and holds them without them costing you effort.
buildings.story: Bunks, a rack and a yard to drill in. Fed workers go in and soldiers come out, and the yard is a good deal more of the building than the roof is.

buildings.name: Watchtower
buildings.summary: Cancels one theft or raid event per game against the town it stands in, and reveals adjacent face-down tiles.
buildings.story: One room at the top, a bell, and somebody bored in it. It earns its whole cost on the single night that is not boring, and nobody can tell you in advance which night that will be.

buildings.name: Palisade
buildings.summary: Defenders in this town roll one extra combat die.
buildings.story: Split trunks set in a ditch, sharpened, and leaning very slightly outward. It will not stop an army. It was never meant to: it is there to make one slow down inside bowshot.

buildings.name: Alchemist
buildings.summary: Brews potions from foraged ingredients and mana crystals. Needs an alembic.
buildings.story: Glass, charcoal, and a shelf of jars labelled in a hand only their owner can read. The alembic is the whole trade - without one the room is a kitchen with an expensive smell.

buildings.name: Shrine
buildings.summary: Once per round, re-roll one effort die in this town.
buildings.story: Four posts, a lintel, and a stone somebody stood upright a very long time ago. Nobody agrees what it is for. Everyone touches it on the way past, and the work goes better.

buildings.name: Road
buildings.summary: Built onto a tile. Halves land movement cost through it and allows carts.

buildings.name: Railroad
buildings.summary: Built onto a tile. Fast, high-capacity cargo, and expensive through anything but flat ground.

buildings.name: Bridge
buildings.summary: Carries a road or rail across one water tile.

buildings.name: Harbour
buildings.summary: Lets ships load and unload. Sea routes are slow to set up and very cheap to run.
buildings.story: An arm of stone thrown out into the water, and behind it flat calm on the roughest day. The most expensive thing a coast town ever builds, and the reason there is a coast town at all.

buildings.name: Rail Depot
buildings.summary: The point where a town joins the rail network. Trains can only load here.
buildings.story: A siding, a platform, and a crane it takes two people to swing. Trains will pass a town all day long; this is the thing that makes one stop.
